newsitem.title: FRANCE: French Greens win first seats in parliament.
newsitem.headline: French Greens win first seats in parliament.

text.p: The Greens party won seats in the French parliament for the first time in Sunday's election, gaining a toehold to preach environmental protection, a nuclear-free world and a four-day work week.

Greens leader Dominique Voynet, a 38-year-old doctor and single mother, was among Green deputies elected to the National Assembly in a nation far less concerned by ecology than many north European states.
"This is the first time the Greens are entering the Assembly," Voynet, the party's iron lady, said in a victory speech after securing her own seat in a district in the Jura, eastern France.
Polling institutes projected that the party might capture a total of nine seats in the 577-member Assembly.
"I will argue for us to follow through our logic and enter government," Voynet said. She has been tipped among candidates for the environment portfolio in a Socialist-led government.
Voynet, who won 3.3 percent of the vote in the 1995 presidential election, helped ensure the Greens' breakthrough under a poll pact with the Socialist Party of Lionel Jospin.
Socialists bowed out in 29 districts to give the Greens a clearer run to the National Assembly in return for the ecologists' backing elsewhere.

The party wants France to phase out nuclear weapons and power plants that generate 75 percent of French electricity, one of the highest levels in the world. It wants to shift to renewable sources like solar power or windmills.
It was among the few parties to strongly oppose President Jacques Chirac's programme of six nuclear tests in 1995-96 in the South Pacific that triggered outrage abroad.
The party wants a huge shift from road to rail in goods transport and a moratorium on building new autoroutes.
It proposes curbing car use in cities to combat air pollution. It wants more ecologically friendly agriculture and seeks to push resources into cleaning up the environment.

It also wants a "massive, rapid and general reduction in working hours" to a four-day week of 32 hours. The plan goes far beyond the 35-hour week, compared to 39 at present, proposed by the Socialists to create jobs.

The party would push for a review of the European Union to redirect efforts towards North-South cooperation. It is not in principle against a single currency. The Greens would halt fiscal austerity policies and forgive foreign debts.
Nuclear power in France has broad support. But building of new plants, such as in the Loire estuary in northwest France, is attracting wider protests.
Official French policy has often seemed anti-environment.

In 1985, France sent secret agents to New Zealand to sink the Greenpeace flagship Rainbow Warrior in Auckland harbour, killing a photographer. In 1986, nuclear safety officials played down the Chernobyl disaster in Ukraine, wrongly saying the cloud of radioactive waste had stopped at France's borders.
